content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies the problem of overfitted trading systems in financial markets, and more specifically the cryptocurrency markets.  First, a trading system is designed and tested using various benchmarks and methodologies.  Second, the paper proposes a novel method for estimating the probability of overfitting generated by each model in order to address the problem of rampant overfitting in trading systems and “existing works” in general.  This method proposes a quantitative metric that relies on “an estimated probability of overfitting to determine whether a trained agent is acceptable” and the use of a hypothesis test.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
Identifies the problem of overfitting in financial system backtesting.
Provides detailed critiques of current methods which lead to overfitting and lack of reproducibility.
Provides a novel solution by creating a quantitative metric to compare models and assess relative overfitting between models.  In theory, such a metric could provide useful information in the trading systems world and make the research process more efficient.

Weaknesses
The trading system itself seems to be limited and based on extremely limited data.
According to the paper, it appears the trading system itself uses information from the future during the test period.  There is no circumstance in any environment where information from the future should be used in a system.   
The models rely on levels of the “CVIX” during training and testing as a risk management tool.  According to the paper:  
“Volatility index CVIX (Crypto VIX) (Bonaparte, 2021b): the total market capitalization of the
crypto market crashed two times in our testing period, namely, 05/06/2022 - 05/12/2022 and
06/09/2022 - 06/15/2022. We take the average CVIX value over those time frames as our threshold,
CVIXt = 90.1.”
Also:
“Figures 6 and 7 give an overview of the trading cumulative return curves for conventional agents,
and for different DRL algorithms, respectively. The timespans are from 05/01/2022 to 06/27/2022,
with an initial trading capital of $1, 000, 000. Note that trading stops as soon as CVIX surpasses the
90.1 threshold.”
For example, if data from the second time frame was being used to test the model on 05/02/2022 (for example), this would not be realistic.  The average level of the CVIX during the training period was 72.7 with a maximum value of 86.5 while the average level of the CVIX during the test period was 88.8 with a maximum value of 124.9.  This implies that information from a future testing period was used during the actual test because the authors state that their threshold was some type of average resulting in a level of 90.1
Because it appears these trading systems might have used information from the future to generate the results, it is very difficult to assess whether the overfitting metric works or not because the systems themselves would not be usable.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity:
The paper is clear on its methodology and contribution as well as demonstrating the need for a quantitative metric for system backtests.
The trading systems themselves, however, seem a bit vague in design.  For example:
1)	Why use a walk forward method and not an expanding window?
2)	Why were these particular features chosen and what is the rationale for each technical indicator?
3)	Why is the data set so small from a very limited time period?   Financial markets are notorious for completely changing their profile instantaneously so in general anything that works during one time period very likely will not work during another time period.

Quality:
The work is well documented with minimal syntax and spelling errors.
The paper does a good job of providing detailed information about the inputs into the model.
However, if the backtests actually use information from the future then all of this needs to be redone to make a proper assessment.

Novelty and Originality
Overfitting is a plague on financial trading system development so the creation of an easily calculated metric to assess model overfitting could be useful in both research and deployment environments.

Reproducibility
This is not possible without the code and exact environment.  Also, the exact pricing data and feature set would be needed.
content.summary_of_the_review: Based on the available information, it appears that the paper relies on models that use information from the future to generate backtest results.  Unless it can be shown that this is not the case, then the evaluation of a novel quantitative metric measuring overfitting is suspect.  I would not recommend this paper unless the model mechanics can be clarified.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this work, the authors propose a practical approach to address backtest overfitting for cryptocurrency trading using deep reinforcement learning, which outperforms walk-forward (WF) and k-fold cross-validation (KVF) when applied to PPO.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
* Strength

(i) The work is easy to follow and overfitting problem hidden from backtest is significant.

(ii) From Table 3, we can see some noticeable improvements.

* Weakness

(i) Only PPO is fully evaluated, along with PPO WF and PPO KCV, and we should have TD3 WF/KCV as well as SAC WF/KCV.

(ii) The technical contribution is quite limited, and application is very focused on crypt-currency trading.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The clarity and quality is fairly good, but novelty is limited. The work is hard to reproduce given the limited access to the same data source.
content.summary_of_the_review: This submission is more like a technical report and not suitable for the ML venue like ICLR.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This work proposes a DRL-based algorithm to handle the backtest overfitting issue in cryptocurrency trading. The problem is first formulated as a hypothesis test problem. The DRL agents are then trained. Finally, the algorithm is evaluated based on test data collected on a crypto market. The results show that DRL-based method results in less overfitting.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength 
- The problem in consideration is interesting and may be relevant in practice. 

Weakness 
- The key question posed in the intro does not seem to directly link to the method proposed. Is there an implicit connection between backtest overfitting and reproducibility? 
- While the application is valid and important, There is not much algorithmic contribution. In fact, as stated in the paper, the authors “pick the DRL agent with the best performing hyperparameters”. This makes the contribution limited. 
- The presentation of the paper should be improved. For instance, the notion of overfitted comes in page 6. Many of the results are also not properly discussed or explained.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The presentation and writing of the paper should be improved. The contribution also needs better highlight. The technical contribution is limited.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper considers an interesting application. However, the algorithmic contribution is limited. Due to the presentation of the paper, it is also hard to directly see the significance of the results.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.
